mode_lightweight_hint: Lightest: alerts on audit and system events, firewall tampering and ransomware protection. No traffic is kept: traffic reports and the workbench query the PCE when you use them (slower, and only as far back as the PCE keeps traffic). Lateral-movement detection, traffic alerts and anomaly detection need alert mode.
mode_full_hint: Everything: lateral-movement detection, the workbench and traffic reports. Traffic is kept 35 days by default and the last 30 days are read back when a PCE is connected.

rpt_unm_candidates_intro: Private addresses that talked to {n} or more managed hosts: installing a VEN there makes their traffic visible and enforceable.
rpt_unm_intro: An address is unmanaged when no VEN reports from it; only its traffic with managed hosts is seen.
rpt_unm_why_admin: A host without a VEN reaching management ports cannot be watched or contained by the PCE.
rpt_unm_action_admin: Find the owner; install a VEN or restrict management ports to known admin hosts.
rpt_mail_no_link: No GUI address is set (Settings → Reports), so this email has no link.
rpt_mail_xlsx_too_large: The XLSX is too large to attach (over {mb} MB together); download it from the Reports page.
gui_reports_err_running: The report is being made; delete it after it finishes.
gui_reports_day_of_month_hint: In a shorter month it runs on the last day.
gui_reports_desc_lateral_posture: Exposure now and after enforcement, critical assets and where to cut, this period's detections, cross-environment and directory traffic.
gui_reports_desc_new_connections: Connections never seen before in the baseline, by port and destination, management ports first.
gui_reports_desc_unmanaged: Addresses without a VEN that talk to managed hosts: VEN candidates, management ports, internet addresses.
gui_reports_email_needs_smtp: Email needs the SMTP channel turned on:
gui_reports_external_url_hint: The address people use to open illumio-ops (for example https://illumio-ops.example.com:5443). Report emails link to it; left empty, emails carry no link.
gui_reports_group_analysis: Analysis: where the risk and the changes are
gui_reports_group_assessment: Assessment: how far policy has come
gui_reports_group_inventory: Inventory: what is there and who talks to whom
gui_reports_retention_hint: Older reports and their files are deleted once a day.
rpt_new_older_than_baseline: The baseline keeps only connections seen in the last {days} days, so connections that first appeared earlier in this period and then stopped are not counted.
rpt_new_left_out: {n} new connections on dynamic ports ({port} and up) or without a port (such as ICMP) are not counted.
rpt_no_flows_filtered: No traffic in this period matches the report's filter.
rpt_field_coverage: Of the period's connections, {process}% carry a process, {user}% a user and {bytes}% byte counts; rankings by these cover only that share.
rpt_err_lookback_beyond_retention: The period is longer than the traffic kept (Data collection > retention); choose fewer days.
rpt_err_app_required: This report is about one application: choose an app label.
rpt_rule_b001_rec_critical_cross_env: CRITICAL: Cross-environment flows on critical ports with explicit allow rules detected. Remove or tightly scope these allow rules immediately. No cross-environment traffic should be permitted on lateral movement ports without a documented exception process. Ports involved: {named_ports}.
rpt_rule_b001_rec_pb_cross_env: CRITICAL: Cross-environment flows detected with no allow rule (potentially_blocked). No explicit policy permits this traffic — it flows only because workloads are in test mode. Move workloads to enforced mode to activate default-deny and block these paths immediately. Investigate why this cross-env traffic exists on: {named_ports}.
rpt_rule_b002_rec: 1) Verify each allowed flow has a documented business justification. 2) Block TeamViewer (5938) and VNC (5900/5901) unless required for specific admin workflows — replace with MFA-protected jump servers. 3) If NetBIOS (137-139) is allowed, migrate to SMBv3 over 445 with encryption. 4) Create Illumio deny rules for these ports from all non-admin workloads.
rpt_rule_b003_rec: 1) Prioritize moving workloads with potentially_blocked flows to enforced mode — start with the highest-risk ports (SSH, NFS). 2) Review the 'potentially_blocked' flows to ensure no legitimate traffic will break when enforcement is applied. 3) Create allow rules for verified legitimate traffic before switching to enforced mode. 4) Set a deadline for enforcement — prolonged test mode leaves the network exposed.
rpt_rule_b004_rec: 1) Identify each unmanaged source IP — are they network devices, legacy servers, or shadow IT? 2) Deploy VEN agents on servers that should be managed. 3) For network devices that can't run a VEN, use IP lists and enforcement boundaries to control their access. 4) Create explicit deny rules for any unmanaged-to-managed path that isn't required.
rpt_rule_b005_rec: 1) Focus first on critical tiers: databases, identity infrastructure (AD/LDAP), and externally-facing workloads. 2) Use Illumio's Explorer to identify top unruled flows and create allow rules for verified traffic. 3) Set a target coverage of >{threshold}% within 30 days. 4) Enable enforcement gradually — start with ring-fencing high-value assets, then expand to general workloads.
rpt_rule_b006_rec_allowed: 1) Investigate the top source IPs — check for exploit tools, unexpected SSH sessions, or RDP brute-force. 2) Remove or tightly scope the allow rules driving the high-fan-out flows. 3) Ring-fence high-value assets (databases, domain controllers) to limit blast radius.
rpt_rule_b006_rec_pb: 1) Investigate the top source IPs — check for exploit tools, unexpected SSH sessions, or RDP brute-force. 2) Move workloads to enforced mode — no allow rules exist for these paths; default-deny will block them upon enforcement. 3) Ring-fence high-value assets (databases, domain controllers) to limit blast radius.
rpt_rule_b007_rec: 1) Cross-reference flagged accounts with HR/IT records — are these admin accounts or regular users? 2) Check authentication logs for failed login attempts or impossible-travel alerts. 3) For admin accounts, enforce just-in-time access and MFA for lateral sessions. 4) Create Illumio user-based rules to limit which destinations each role can access. 5) If compromise is suspected, rotate credentials immediately and isolate the workload.
rpt_rule_b008_rec: 1) Verify the flows behind this outlier — are they backup servers, replication, or database sync? Document expected high-volume flows. 2) For unexplained transfers, check if the source is a compromised workload exfiltrating data to an external or lateral destination. 3) Consider volume-aware rules or QoS policies for known high-volume services. 4) Set up Illumio monitoring alerts for sustained anomalous volume.
rpt_rule_b009_rec: 1) Audit each cross-env flow pair — document which ones are expected (e.g., Production monitoring pulling from Staging). 2) Create explicit Illumio rules for approved cross-env paths with specific port restrictions. 3) Block all other cross-env flows, especially database ports (see L004) and admin protocols (SSH, RDP). 4) Use Illumio environment labels consistently to enforce isolation boundaries.
rpt_rule_l001_rec: Immediately disable Telnet (port 23) and FTP (ports 20/21). Replace with SSH (22) or SFTP. Cleartext credentials can be captured by any attacker with network access, enabling trivial lateral movement.
rpt_rule_l002_rec: Block NetBIOS (137-138), LLMNR (5355), and SSDP (1900) at the segmentation layer. These protocols serve no legitimate role in modern micro-segmented environments and are used almost exclusively for network reconnaissance and credential poisoning attacks (e.g., Responder / Inveigh).
rpt_rule_l003_rec: Database ports should only be reachable from their direct application tier (typically 1-2 app labels). Use Illumio rule-sets to restrict db access to approved app labels only. Wide database exposure is the primary post-exploitation data exfiltration path after lateral movement succeeds.
rpt_rule_l004_rec: Enforce strict environment isolation for all database ports. No Dev/Test/Staging application should have direct access to Production databases. Use read replicas or API gateways as the cross-environment interface, never direct DB ports.
rpt_rule_l005_rec_allowed: Restrict Kerberos (88) and LDAP (389/636) to domain-joined workloads only. Remove or tightly scope allow rules permitting broad identity-port access. No application tier should query LDAP directly — use a service account wrapper.
rpt_rule_l005_rec_pb: These flows have no allow rule — move workloads to enforced mode so default-deny blocks them. Before enforcing, create allow rules only for legitimate LDAP consumers (domain-joined workloads). No application tier should query LDAP directly — use a service account wrapper.
rpt_rule_l007_rec: Unmanaged hosts should NEVER directly reach database, identity, or Windows management ports. Options: (1) Onboard the hosts to PCE immediately, (2) Add explicit deny rules for unmanaged sources on these ports, (3) Investigate whether these are attacker-controlled hosts or shadow IT. Priority: verify the top source IPs are known/authorised assets.
rpt_rule_l008_rec: Move workloads from visibility/test mode to selective or full enforcement. Until enforcement is active, 'potentially_blocked' flows are live attack paths — no allow rule covers them; only enforced mode's default-deny will block them. Check enforcement mode in PCE for the destination apps: {top_apps}.
rpt_rule_l009_rec: Investigate all managed-to-unmanaged outbound flows above the threshold. Legitimate outbound traffic (internet APIs, CDN) should be explicitly allowed and scoped to known destination IPs or ranges. Apply an outbound allowlist policy and deny all other external destinations. Top suspicious destinations (by bytes): {top_dst_fmt}.
rpt_rule_l010_rec: CRITICAL: Lateral movement ports (SMB 445, RDP 3389, WinRM 5985/5986, RPC 135) must NEVER be allowed across environment boundaries. Implement deny rules at the environment boundary level immediately. This represents an active lateral movement path between environments that an attacker can exploit to escalate from low-security to high-security zones.
rpt_rule_b001_how: Checks for traffic on ransomware's primary attack ports (SMB 445, RPC 135, RDP 3389, WinRM 5985/5986) that is NOT blocked. These are the exact ports used in EternalBlue, NotPetya, and WannaCry-class attacks for network-wide lateral spread.
rpt_rule_b002_how: Detects allowed flows on secondary remote-access ports (TeamViewer 5938, VNC 5900, NetBIOS 137-139). Ransomware operators and APT groups use these for C2 persistence and remote control after initial compromise.
rpt_rule_b003_how: Counts potentially blocked flows on medium-risk ports (SSH 22, NFS 2049, FTP 20/21, Telnet 23, HTTP 80, mDNS, LLMNR, SSDP, WS-Discovery). No rule covers them: they pass today only because the destination is not enforced.
rpt_rule_b004_how: Counts flows from hosts not enrolled in the PCE. Unmanaged hosts have no VEN and therefore no micro-segmentation enforcement — they are outside the zero-trust boundary and represent uncontrolled attack surface.
rpt_rule_b005_how: Measures the share of observed flows that an allow rule covers. Below the configured threshold (30% by default), most traffic is uncontrolled — segmentation is in early stages and a large attack surface remains.
rpt_rule_b006_how: Detects sources that reach an unusually high number of distinct destinations on the management (remote-execution) ports set under Lateral settings. This fan-out (one source → many destinations) is the hallmark of worm propagation and hands-on-keyboard pivoting.
rpt_rule_b007_how: Detects individual user accounts connecting to unusually many unique destination IPs. This may indicate a compromised account being used for automated reconnaissance, credential stuffing, or data staging before exfiltration.
rpt_rule_b008_how: Totals each source → destination × service over the period and flags those above the configured percentile, the configured multiple of the median and the configured minimum size (95th, 10×, 1 MB by default). Only flows that carry byte counts are compared. Sudden high-volume transfers from unexpected sources are a key indicator of data staging or exfiltration.
rpt_rule_b009_how: Tracks the number of flows crossing environment boundaries (e.g. Production → Development). Excessive cross-env traffic may indicate lateral movement from a compromised lower-security zone into production.
rpt_rule_l001_how: Detects any traffic on Telnet (23) or FTP (20/21). These protocols transmit credentials and data without encryption. Any attacker with network access can perform a man-in-the-middle or ARP poisoning attack to harvest passwords in plaintext — enabling instant credential reuse for lateral movement.
rpt_rule_l002_how: Detects unblocked flows on broadcast/discovery protocols: NetBIOS (137/138), mDNS (5353), LLMNR (5355), SSDP (1900). Tools like Responder and Inveigh exploit these to perform hostname poisoning and capture NTLMv2 hashes without any authentication — then crack or relay those hashes for lateral movement.
rpt_rule_l003_name: Database Port Accessible from Many App Tiers
rpt_rule_l003_how: Checks whether database ports (MSSQL 1433, MySQL 3306, PostgreSQL 5432, Oracle 1521, MongoDB 27017, Redis 6379, Elasticsearch 9200) are reachable from many distinct application labels. Databases should only be reachable from their direct app tier. Wide exposure provides direct data access after a single lateral move.
rpt_rule_l004_how: Detects allowed database flows crossing environment boundaries (e.g. Dev app → Production database). Environment boundaries are the macro-segmentation layer. Breaching them allows an attacker in a low-security Dev environment to directly access Production data stores.
rpt_rule_l005_how: Detects Kerberos (88), LDAP (389/636), and Global Catalog (3268/3269) traffic from many source applications. Active Directory is the domain's authentication authority. Excessive access enables domain enumeration (BloodHound), Kerberoasting, Golden/Silver Ticket attacks, and full domain takeover.
rpt_rule_l006_how: Reads the exposure analysis: for each host, how many other hosts it can reach now through chains of allowed management-port connections. A host that reaches many others is a high-value pivot — compromising it opens all of them.
rpt_rule_l007_how: Detects unmanaged (non-PCE) hosts communicating on database, identity (Kerberos/LDAP), or Windows management ports to managed workloads. Unmanaged hosts have no VEN enforcement — they are outside zero-trust. If they can reach critical services, they represent uncontrolled lateral movement entry points.
rpt_rule_l008_name: Lateral Ports in Test Mode — Policy Not Enforced
rpt_rule_l008_how: Counts potentially blocked flows on management, database and identity ports. These paths have no allow rule and pass only because the destination is not enforced — each one is a live lateral-movement path until enforcement starts.
rpt_rule_l009_name: Data Exfiltration Pattern — Outbound to Unmanaged
rpt_rule_l009_how: Detects managed workloads transferring significant data volume to unmanaged (external/unknown) destinations. This is the post-lateral-movement exfiltration phase: attacker has pivoted to a high-value host and is now staging or exfiltrating data to an external C2 or drop server outside PCE visibility.
rpt_rule_l010_name: Cross-Environment Lateral Port Access — Boundary Break
rpt_rule_l010_how: Detects allowed flows on management ports (the configured remote-execution ports plus SMB, RPC and WinRM) between different environments. Environment segmentation is the macro-security boundary; if management ports cross it, one compromised environment opens the others.
rpt_rule_b001_rec_allowed: Allowed flows on critical ports inside one environment are typical of Windows administration, and are also how ransomware spreads. Verify each source is an authorised admin system or jump host, then scope the allow rules to those sources. Ports involved: {named_ports}.
rpt_rule_b001_rec_pb: Flows on critical ports inside one environment have no allow rule (potentially blocked): they pass only because the destination is not enforced. Verify the sources, write allow rules for authorised admin systems only, then enforce. Ports involved: {named_ports}.
rpt_rule_l006_rec: Reduce allowed management-port paths so each host reaches only what it must administer. Start with the hosts listed, scope their allow rules to named jump hosts, and recheck the exposure graph.
rpt_rule_b001_desc: {n_total} flows on critical ports were not blocked ({n_allowed} allowed, {n_pb} potentially blocked); {n_cross_env} crossed environments. Ports: {named_ports}. Top destinations: {top_destinations}.
rpt_rule_b002_desc: {n_flows} allowed flows from {unique_src} sources on secondary remote-access ports. Ports: {named_ports}. Top destinations: {top_destinations}.
rpt_rule_b003_desc: {n_flows} potentially blocked flows from {unique_src} sources on medium-risk ports. Ports: {named_ports}. Top destinations: {top_destinations}.
rpt_rule_b004_desc: {n_flows} flows came from unmanaged sources (threshold {threshold}). Top sources: {top_sources}.
rpt_rule_b005_desc: Only {coverage_pct}% of {n_flows} flows are covered by an allow rule (threshold {threshold}%).
rpt_rule_b006_desc: {n_sources} sources reached more than {threshold} distinct destinations on management ports. Top sources (destinations): {top_sources}.
rpt_rule_b007_desc: {n_users} users reached more than {threshold} distinct destinations. Top users (destinations): {top_users}.
rpt_rule_b008_desc: {n_outliers} of {n_with_bytes} source → destination pairs carried more than {limit_mb} MB in the period. Largest: {top_pairs}.
rpt_rule_b009_desc: {n_flows} flows crossed environments (threshold {threshold}). Top environment pairs: {top_pairs}.
rpt_rule_l001_desc: {n_flows} flows on cleartext protocols ({n_allowed} allowed). Ports: {named_ports}.
rpt_rule_l002_desc: {n_flows} unblocked flows on discovery protocols (threshold {threshold}). Ports: {named_ports}.
rpt_rule_l003_desc: {n_targets} database services were reached by more than {threshold} distinct source apps. Top (source apps): {top_targets}.
rpt_rule_l004_desc: {n_flows} allowed database flows crossed environments. Top destinations: {top_destinations}.
rpt_rule_l006_desc: {n_hosts} hosts can reach at least {threshold} other hosts over allowed management paths. Top (hosts reachable): {top_hosts}.
rpt_rule_l007_desc: {n_flows} unblocked flows from unmanaged sources to database, identity or Windows management ports. Ports: {named_ports}. Top sources: {top_sources}.
rpt_rule_l008_desc: {n_flows} potentially blocked flows on management, database and identity ports (threshold {threshold}). Top destination apps: {top_apps}.
rpt_rule_l009_desc: Managed workloads sent {total_mb} MB to unmanaged destinations over allowed flows (threshold {threshold} MB). Top destinations: {top_dst_fmt}.
rpt_rule_l010_desc: {n_flows} allowed management-port flows crossed environments. Ports: {named_ports}. Environment pairs: {top_pairs}.
gui_reports_desc_traffic: What moved in the period: flows and connections by decision, the busiest apps, environments, services and host pairs, and rule-based findings.
rpt_trf_decisions_intro: A flow is one connection record; its connections are how many times that source, destination and service connected. Into managed hosts counts flows whose destination has a VEN, whoever started them.
rpt_trf_bytes_intro: {pct}% of the period's flows carry byte counts; this ranking covers only those.
rpt_trf_no_bytes: No flow in the period carries byte counts, so there is no transfer ranking. Byte counts come only from VENs that report them.
rpt_trf_unmanaged: Of {total} flows, {from_n} came from addresses without a VEN and {to_n} went to one.
rpt_trf_unmanaged_see: The Unmanaged endpoints report lists each address: VEN candidates, management ports, internet addresses.
rpt_trf_findings_intro: Rules carried over from the 5.x traffic report, evaluated on this period's flows. Thresholds are under Settings → Reports.
rpt_trf_quality_counts: Flows are connection records; connections are the connection counts they carry. Labels are those at the time of each flow.
rpt_rule_error: This rule could not be evaluated ({error}); the other rules ran.
rpt_rules_none_fired: No rule fired in this period.
gui_reports_desc_security_risk: How far segmentation has come and where the risk is: maturity score, policy coverage, traffic no rule covers, enforcement progress by app, ransomware and lateral summaries, rule findings.
rpt_sec_maturity_none: No part of the score has data yet (no managed hosts, no traffic, no ransomware data).
rpt_sec_no_hosts: No managed host in the inventory matches this report.
rpt_sec_rw_no_data: No ransomware ratings from the PCE.
rpt_sec_detections_all_hosts: All hosts, whatever the report's filter.
rpt_sec_coverage_intro: Allowed: an allow rule covers the flow. Potentially blocked: no rule covers it and the destination is not enforced, so it passes today and would be blocked once enforced. Blocked: dropped by enforcement.
rpt_sec_direction_coverage: Of flows into managed hosts, {inbound} are allowed by a rule; of flows out of managed hosts, {outbound}.
rpt_sec_uncovered_intro: Potentially blocked and blocked connections by source and destination app: each pair needs a rule or a decision that it should stay blocked.
rpt_sec_advice_unlabeled: The source has no app label: label it, or onboard it with a VEN if it is unmanaged, then write the rule.
rpt_sec_advice_same_app: Within the same app: add an intra-app rule for the services the app's tiers really use.
rpt_sec_advice_cross_app: Between two apps: add a rule between them for the needed services only, or confirm it should be blocked.
rpt_sec_enforcement_intro: Managed hosts by app and environment and their enforcement mode, from the current inventory. Enforced counts full and selective.
rpt_sec_pb_intro: Connections that pass today only because the destination is not enforced, by destination app and service, with the rule each needs before enforcement.
rpt_sec_tbl_pb: Potentially blocked connections by destination app and service
rpt_sec_pb_rule: In {app}'s ruleset, allow {service} from the sources that need it.
rpt_sec_pb_rule_unlabeled: Label the destination first; then allow {service} from the sources that need it.
rpt_sec_rw_none: No unprotected service with recent traffic.
rpt_sec_rw_not_computed: The ransomware analysis has not been computed yet (it runs hourly once the inventory is collected).
rpt_sec_rw_unsupported: This PCE does not provide ransomware ratings.
rpt_sec_rw_see: The Ransomware protection report lists every host and service.
rpt_sec_users_intro: {user}% of the period's flows carry the initiating user and {process}% the initiating process; these rankings cover only those.
rpt_sec_no_users: No flow in the period carries a user, so there is no user ranking. Users come only from VENs that report them.
rpt_sec_no_processes: No flow in the period carries a process, so there is no process ranking.
rpt_sec_lateral_detections: {n} lateral-movement detections were first seen in the period ({high} high or critical).
rpt_sec_lateral_exposure: Now: {assets} critical assets reachable, {pivots} pivot hosts, {cross_env} cross-environment paths.
rpt_sec_lateral_see: The {report} report has the paths, pivots and detections.
gui_reports_desc_network_inventory: How the estate is labelled and how apps depend on each other: label hygiene, app-to-app dependencies, services each app provides, unmanaged sources into apps.
rpt_inv_hygiene_intro: Managed hosts in the current inventory without one of these labels: {keys}. Rules written by label cannot reach a host that lacks them.
rpt_inv_unlabeled_flows: {n} flows in the period had a managed end without an app label.
rpt_inv_env_mix: {same} connections stayed within one {key}, {cross} crossed between {key} values and {unknown} had an end without a {key} label.
rpt_inv_services_intro: For each destination app: its connections, the busiest services it provides and how many source apps use it.
rpt_inv_pairs_limit: Computed from the {n} busiest app × service and app × source-app pairs.
rpt_inv_tbl_unmanaged: Connections from unmanaged sources by destination app
rpt_inv_unmanaged_none: No unmanaged source reached a managed host in this period.
rpt_inv_quality_inventory: Label hygiene and host counts are from the current inventory, not the period.
gui_reports_desc_app_summary: One application: its inbound, outbound and intra-app traffic, policy impact, hosts and enforcement, uncovered traffic and rule findings. Choose the app in the filter.
rpt_app_inbound_intro: Traffic into the app from other apps and addresses, by source app and service.
rpt_app_tbl_inbound: Inbound connections by source app and service
rpt_app_outbound_intro: Traffic from the app to other apps and addresses, by destination app and service.
rpt_app_tbl_outbound: Outbound connections by destination app and service
rpt_app_impact_text: {allowed} of the app's connections are allowed by a rule; {pb} flows are potentially blocked and would be blocked once the app is enforced.
rpt_app_hosts_intro: Managed hosts in the current inventory whose labels match the app exactly.
rpt_app_no_hosts: No managed host in the inventory has this app's labels.
rpt_app_findings_intro: The rules evaluated on this app's flows only (both directions), with the same thresholds as the other reports.
rpt_app_quality_split: Inbound, outbound and intra-app traffic are counted once each: intra-app traffic is not repeated on either side. The app is matched exactly as the PCE names it.
rpt_err_filter_not_supported: This report type does not take a filter; it always covers every host.
gui_reports_filter_hint: Optional: narrow the report to hosts with these labels. Without a filter it covers every host.
gui_reports_filter_app_required: Choose the app this report is about (an app label on either side); an environment may narrow it.
gui_reports_filter_no_labels: No labels yet: the inventory has not been collected.
gui_reports_filter_truncated: Only the first 500 values are listed.
rpt_rules_not_evaluated: The rules were not evaluated: no traffic in the period matches this report.
rpt_err_app_filter_shape: An app summary needs the app named on one side only, with no conditions on the other side and no excluded or individual hosts; use the traffic report for other filters.
gui_reports_desc_ven_status: Which VENs are online, which went quiet and when, which do not have their policy, the fleet's versions, systems and modes, and tampering no known cause explains.
rpt_ven_problem_behind: received a newer policy than it applied
rpt_ven_offline_intro: A VEN is online when the PCE marks it online and its last heartbeat is under an hour old; the rest are grouped by how long ago they last reported. A host whose heartbeat was never collected is counted apart, not as offline.
rpt_ven_none_offline: Every VEN with a known heartbeat reported in the last hour.
rpt_ven_sync_intro: Online VENs whose policy is not in place: not applied yet, firewall configuration not current, a newer policy received than applied, never applied, or agent health errors.
rpt_ven_tbl_sync: Online VENs with policy sync problems
rpt_ven_none_sync: No online VEN has a policy sync problem.
rpt_ven_none_hosts: No managed host in the inventory.
rpt_ven_tamper_intro: Hosts whose VEN reported tampering in the last 60 days, most unexplained first. A reading a known cause explains (an annotation on the host page) is not counted as unexplained.
rpt_ven_none_tamper: No VEN reported tampering in the last 60 days.
rpt_ven_tamper_known: {n} known causes are recorded; each host page shows which readings they explain.
rpt_ven_tamper_not_computed: The tampering summary has not been computed yet (it runs hourly once events are collected).
rpt_ven_quality_inventory: Inventory as collected at {at}; the report shows the current state, not the period's.
rpt_ven_quality_no_inventory: The inventory has not been collected yet.
rpt_ven_quality_online: Online = marked online by the PCE and a heartbeat in the last hour. Version, operating system and mode each come from one inventory field.
rpt_ven_quality_unknown: The VEN status of {n} hosts has not been collected yet (it arrives with the next inventory run); they are not counted as offline.
gui_reports_desc_audit: What happened on the PCE: the event types that matter by risk, who did what and who failed to sign in, policy provisions, agent security events and brute force.
rpt_aud_attention_intro: Event types with an audit risk (5.x levels), most serious first, with the users behind them.
rpt_aud_none_attention: No event with an audit risk in this period.
rpt_aud_action_critical: Investigate now: confirm each event was expected, starting with the host or user named.
rpt_aud_action_high: Review each event with its owner and confirm it was authorised.
rpt_aud_action_medium: Check the changes against your change records.
rpt_aud_action_low: Note the pattern; act if it keeps growing.
rpt_aud_users_intro: Users and service accounts only: events made by the system or by VENs are not counted under anyone.
rpt_aud_none_users: No user or service account made a change in this period.
rpt_aud_none_failed: No failed sign-in in this period.
rpt_aud_none_provisions: No policy was provisioned in this period.
rpt_aud_tbl_agent: Tampering, clones, suspended and unpaired agents
rpt_aud_none_agent: No agent security event in this period.
rpt_aud_agent_see: The VEN status report shows each host's tampering and the known causes recorded for it.
rpt_aud_brute_intro: A source address with at least 5 failed sign-ins within 30 minutes.
rpt_aud_tbl_brute: Source addresses with repeated failed sign-ins
rpt_aud_none_brute: No source address failed to sign in 5 times within 30 minutes.
rpt_aud_quality_whole: Events were collected for the whole period.
rpt_aud_quality_gaps: Events are missing for {n} stretches of the period; counts there are incomplete.
rpt_aud_quality_actors: Users are users and service accounts; the system and VENs are never counted as a user.
gui_reports_desc_ransomware: The PCE's ransomware judgement taken apart: what to fix first, what to block now, what looks suspicious, each host's score and the allow rules behind it, and the trend.
rpt_rw_kpi_contradictions: Hosts whose PCE score contradicts its services
rpt_rw_not_computed: The ransomware analysis has not been computed yet (it runs hourly once the inventory is collected).
rpt_rw_unsupported: This PCE does not provide ransomware ratings.
rpt_rw_org_missing: The PCE's organisation summary has not been read yet.
rpt_rw_priority_intro: Unprotected, listening and used in the last 30 days: closing these needs a rule for the sources that use them.
rpt_rw_safe_intro: Unprotected and listening but unused in the last 30 days: blocking them affects no one seen.
rpt_rw_suspicious_intro: Unprotected and not listening, yet something tried to connect.
rpt_rw_none_priority: No unprotected service with recent traffic.
rpt_rw_none_safe: No unprotected listening service without traffic.
rpt_rw_none_suspicious: No connection attempt to a service that is not listening.
rpt_rw_hosts_intro: Each host's score as the PCE gives it and as its own services add up (approximate: the PCE gives each service's protection state, not its exact coverage). Allowed sources still count as attack surface — that is the vendor's deliberate design. Hosts whose PCE score contradicts their services are listed last and not ranked.
rpt_rw_none_hosts: No host has a ransomware rating.
rpt_rw_allow_intro: For the hosts at the top of the fix-first list: the allow rules that let sources reach each service, from the PCE's rule search.
rpt_rw_allow_error: The PCE's rule search could not be read; this is not "no allow rule".
rpt_rw_allow_partial: Only part of the answer: an end of the rule could not be placed.
rpt_rw_none_allow: No service on the fix-first list.
rpt_rw_allow_top: Only the first {n} hosts of the fix-first list are looked up (one rule search per service).
rpt_rw_trend_intro: Per day, the share of critical and high services with a known protection state that are protected, from the daily snapshots.
rpt_rw_none_trend: No daily snapshot in this period.
rpt_rw_quality_source: Services, severities, protection states and exposure are the PCE's own judgement; the three lists add the last 30 days of collected traffic.
rpt_rw_quality_approx: The score from each host's services is approximate: the PCE gives a protection state per service, not its exact coverage.
rpt_rw_quality_contradictions: {n} hosts have a PCE score that contradicts their services; they are flagged and not ranked.
gui_reports_desc_readiness: For each app, whether it can move to enforcement: five factors over the traffic into it and its hosts' modes, what the draft policy would block, and the order to enforce in.
rpt_rdy_no_apps: No app has traffic into its hosts or managed hosts in this period.
rpt_rdy_advice_policy: Write allow rules for the traffic into the app that has none.
rpt_rdy_advice_ringfence: Define the app's ring-fence: which apps may reach it, on which services.
rpt_rdy_advice_enforcement: Move the app's hosts to selective or full enforcement.
rpt_rdy_advice_staged: Review the potentially blocked traffic: write rules for what is needed before enforcing.
rpt_rdy_advice_remote: Scope the remote-access traffic (SSH, RDP, WinRM) to the admin sources that need it.
rpt_rdy_advice_ready: Ready: enforce, then watch the blocked traffic for a few days.
rpt_rdy_scores_intro: Every app, highest score first. “Why” names the factor losing the most points and what the score would be with it at full marks; the factors are explained under “How to read this report”.
rpt_rdy_sec_predicted: What the draft policy would block
rpt_rdy_predicted_intro: The PCE recomputed the period's traffic against the draft policy: connections a deny rule would block, by destination app and rule.
rpt_rdy_predicted_none: The draft policy blocks none of the period's traffic.
rpt_rdy_predicted_capped: The PCE stopped at the {n} rows this report asks for: more traffic may be blocked than shown.
rpt_rdy_predicted_unsupported: This PCE does not recompute traffic against the draft policy.
rpt_rdy_predicted_failed: The draft recompute could not be read from the PCE ({error}); the rest of the report stands.
rpt_rdy_quality_definition: An app's traffic is the connections into its managed hosts; connections are num_connections summed. Labels are matched exactly.
rpt_rdy_quality_unknown: {pct}% of the connections into managed hosts had no reported decision; they are left out of "allowed by a rule" and "not potentially blocked".
rpt_rdy_predicted_undetermined: The PCE gave no draft decision for {n} flows into managed hosts: what the draft would block is not fully known.
rpt_quality_analysis_at: The analysis this report reads was computed at {at}.
rpt_quality_analysis_failed: Its latest run failed ({error}): the results shown are from the last run that succeeded.
rpt_rw_org_last_known: No organisation summary in this period; the last one read is from {day}.
rpt_rdy_advice_not_assessed: Not assessed: no traffic into it in this period.
rpt_rdy_predicted_none_unconfirmed: No blocked connection was found, but some flows had no draft decision: this is not a confirmed "blocks nothing".
rpt_err_ondemand_failed: The PCE could not answer the traffic query for this period. Try again later; if it keeps failing, check the PCE's health and the data collection page.
rpt_quality_ondemand: Traffic was queried from the PCE when the report was made (this install keeps no traffic for the period); labels as they are now, not as they were when the traffic happened.
rpt_quality_ondemand_none: The PCE returned no traffic for the period: it may keep no traffic that old.
rpt_quality_ondemand_earliest: The PCE returned traffic from {start} on: it keeps no older traffic for this period.
rpt_quality_ondemand_capped: Reading stopped at {n} rows: traffic from {start} on is not in this report. A shorter period, or alert or full mode, covers it.
rpt_quality_ondemand_truncated: {n} query window(s) between {start} and {end} reached the PCE's limit and were cut short: connections in them may be missing (a connection missing from the baseline would count as new).
rpt_rule_l006_no_exposure: the exposure graph has not been computed (it needs alert or full mode, or the first hourly analysis)
rpt_rdy_explain: {score} points ({grade}): the most is lost on “{factor}” — {share} of the connections, {got} of its {weight} points. With it at full marks: about {fixed} points.
rpt_rdy_how_intro: Each app gets a score from 0 to 100 for one question: if its hosts were enforced now, would normal traffic be blocked? The higher, the safer to enforce. The score adds up the five factors below by their points; a factor without data is left out and the others scaled up.
rpt_rdy_measures_policy: Of the connections into the app with a reported decision, the share an allow rule permits.
rpt_rdy_measures_ringfence: Of the connections into the app, the share that come from the app itself: the fewer outside sources, the easier to ring-fence.
rpt_rdy_measures_enforcement: Of the app's managed hosts, the share already enforced (selective counts half).
rpt_rdy_measures_staged: Of the connections with a reported decision, the share not reported as potentially blocked, which enforcement would block.
rpt_rdy_measures_remote: Of the remote-access connections (SSH, RDP, WinRM and the like), the share a rule permits.
rpt_rdy_full_policy: Every connection in has a rule.
rpt_rdy_full_ringfence: Every connection in comes from the app itself.
rpt_rdy_full_enforcement: Every host is in full enforcement.
rpt_rdy_full_remote: Every remote-access connection has a rule.
rpt_rdy_means_a: Ready: nearly every connection in has a rule. Enforce, then watch the blocked traffic for a few days.
rpt_rdy_means_b: Close: write rules for the few connections listed under “What to do first”, then enforce.
rpt_rdy_means_c: Rules still missing: work on the factor that loses the most points first.
rpt_rdy_means_d: Most connections have no rule yet: enforcing now would block a lot of normal traffic.
rpt_rdy_means_f: Not started: most connections have no rule and the hosts are not enforced. Start by writing rules.
rpt_rdy_next_intro: The apps closest to enforcement, each with where it stands, the next step, and its busiest connections in that no rule allows yet (reported potentially blocked: enforcement would block them).
rpt_rdy_finding_title: {n} of {total} apps cannot be enforced yet
rpt_rdy_finding_why: Enforcing them now would block normal traffic. The closest is {app}: {explain}
rpt_rdy_finding_action: Follow “What to do first”: it lists, for the closest apps, the connections to write rules for.
rpt_sec_maturity_note: Grade {grade}: the most is lost on “{part}” ({got} of its {weight} points). With it at full marks: about {fixed} points. How it is worked out: “How the maturity score is worked out”.
rpt_sec_sec_how: How the maturity score is worked out
rpt_sec_how_intro: One score from 0 to 100 for how far segmentation has come: are hosts enforced, does policy cover the traffic, are management ports and unmanaged sources kept in check. It adds up the five parts below by their points; a part without data is left out and the others scaled up. “This period” shows where the points were lost.
rpt_sec_measures_enforcement: Of the managed hosts, the share enforced (selective counts half).
rpt_sec_measures_policy: Of the connections with a reported decision, the share an allow rule permits.
rpt_sec_measures_lateral: Connections on management ports (SSH, RDP, SMB…) that were not blocked, against all connections: none scores full, 30% or more scores 0.
rpt_sec_measures_managed: Connections from unmanaged sources (no VEN), against all connections: none scores full, 50% or more scores 0.
rpt_sec_measures_ransomware: Of the critical and high ransomware-risk services the PCE rated, the share protected.
rpt_sec_full_enforcement: Every host is in full enforcement.
rpt_sec_full_lateral: No management-port connection gets through unblocked.
rpt_sec_full_managed: Every connection comes from a managed host.
rpt_sec_full_ransomware: Every critical and high service is protected.
rpt_sec_means_a: In place: most hosts enforced, most traffic covered by rules. Keep watching.
rpt_sec_means_b: Nearly there: close the part that loses the most points.
rpt_sec_means_c: Under way: clear gaps remain; start with the part that loses the most points.
rpt_sec_means_d: Early: most traffic has no rule or most hosts are not enforced.
rpt_sec_means_f: Not started: almost no rules or enforcement, so lateral movement is unrestricted.
rpt_rw_how_intro: Every number here comes from the PCE's own ransomware ratings: which high-risk services (SMB, RDP, WinRM…) each host listens on and whether policy protects them. The three lists say what to do; the scores show where each host stands.
rpt_rw_tbl_terms: What the numbers and lists mean
rpt_rw_term_pce_means: The PCE's own protection score for the host: of its high-risk services, the share protected, weighted by severity. 0–100%, higher is better.
rpt_rw_term_computed_means: The same share, added up here from each service's protection state the PCE reports. The PCE does not give exact coverage, so it is approximate.
rpt_rw_term_computed_use: Where it differs much from the PCE score, go by the service list.
rpt_rw_term_exposure_means: The PCE's ransomware exposure rating for the host (critical, high, medium, low).
rpt_rw_term_exposure_use: Hosts rated critical or high come first.
rpt_rw_term_contradiction_means: The PCE's score and its own list of service states do not match (for example a 0% score with every service protected).
rpt_rw_term_contradiction_use: Not ranked here: check the host's ransomware page on the PCE console.
rpt_rw_term_state_means: Protected: a rule or enforcement stops traffic to the service. Unprotected: any source can reach it. Unknown: the PCE gave no state.
rpt_rw_term_state_use: Unprotected services are the ones in the three lists.
rpt_rw_term_priority_use: Write rules for the sources that use the service, then close it to everyone else.
rpt_rw_term_safe_use: Block it now (a deny rule, or turn the service off): no source seen in 30 days is affected.
rpt_rw_term_suspicious_use: Find out who tries to connect: a scan, or a leftover setting.
rpt_rw_explain_open: {n} high-risk service(s) unprotected ({names}): see this host in “Fix first” and “Safe to block now”.
rpt_rw_explain_contradiction: The PCE scores it {pce}, but its own service list does not match ({n} unprotected): check the host on the PCE console.
rpt_rw_finding_priority: {n} unprotected high-risk service(s) are in use
rpt_rw_finding_priority_why: They are open to any source and were reached in the last 30 days: ransomware can spread through them from those sources.
rpt_rw_finding_priority_action: Follow “Fix first”: write rules for the sources using each service, then close it to everyone else.
rpt_rw_finding_safe: {n} unprotected high-risk service(s) can be blocked now
rpt_rw_finding_safe_why: Nobody reached them in the last 30 days, yet any source could.
rpt_rw_finding_safe_action: Follow “Safe to block now”: a deny rule or turning the service off affects no source seen.
rpt_rw_finding_unsorted: {n} unprotected high-risk service(s) could not be sorted by use
rpt_rw_finding_unsorted_why: Sorting them into “Fix first” and “Safe to block now” needs the last 30 days of traffic, which this install does not keep (lightweight mode).
rpt_rw_finding_unsorted_action: See each host's unprotected services under “Hosts and their scores”; to have them sorted automatically, switch to alert mode on the Data collection page.
rpt_rw_explain_open_unsorted: {n} high-risk service(s) unprotected ({names}). Whether anyone uses them is unknown (no traffic kept), so they are in no list: decide which must stay reachable, and protect the rest.
